user_input: What immunities and privileges are entitled to a witness before a commission of inquiry?
response: A witness before a commission of inquiry is entitled to the same immunities and privileges as if he were a witness before the High Court (Article 283, Chapter TWENTY-THREE, p.183).
retrieved_contexts:
A witness before a commission of inquiry is entitled to the same
immunities and privileges as if he were a witness before the High Court.

(1) A commission of inquiry shall have the powers, rights and privileges
of the High Court or a Justice of the High Court at a trial, in respect of -
(a) enforcing the attendance of witnesses and examining them on
oath, affirmation or otherwise;
(b) compelling the production of documents; and
(c) the issue of a commission or request to examine witnesses
abroad.
(2) A sole commissioner or a member of a commission of inquiry shall
not be liable to any action or suit in respect of any matter or thing done
by him in the performance of his function as a commissioner or member.
reference: A witness before a commission of inquiry is entitled to the same immunities and privileges as if he were a witness before the High Court.

user_input: What is the age threshold for defining a child according to Article 28 of the Ghanaian Constitution?
response:
According to Article 6, Chapter Three, Page 28 of the Ghanaian Constitution, the age thresholds for defining a child in relation to citizenship are as follows:

- A child of not more than seven years of age found in Ghana whose parents are not known is presumed to be a citizen by birth.
- A child of not more than sixteen years of age, neither of whose parents is a citizen of Ghana, who is adopted by a citizen of Ghana shall, by virtue of the adoption, be a citizen of Ghana.

Thus, the age thresholds mentioned are seven years and sixteen years, depending on the context (presumption of citizenship or adoption) (Article 6, Chapter THREE, p.28).
retrieved_contexts:
(1) Every person who, on the coming into force of this Constitution, is a
citizen of Ghana by law shall continue to be a citizen of Ghana.
(2) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, a person born in or
outside Ghana after the coming into force of this Constitution, shall
become a citizen of Ghana at the date of his birth if either of his parents
or grandparents is or was a citizen of Ghana.
(3) A child of not more than seven years of age found in Ghana whose
parents are not know shall be presumed to be a citizen of Ghana by birth.
(4) A child of not more than sixteen years of age neither of whose
parents is a citizen of Ghana who is adopted by a citizen of Ghana shall,
be virtue of the adoption, be a citizen of Ghana.
reference: A child means a person below the age of eighteen years.

user_input: What are the main sections covered regarding the Superior Courts as outlined in this part of the constitution?
response:
The main sections covered regarding the Superior Courts in this part of the constitution include:

1. The composition of the Superior Courts of Judicature, which comprises the Supreme Court, the Court of Appeal, and the High Court and Regional Tribunals (Article 126(1)(a)(i)-(iii)).

2. The status of the Superior Courts as superior courts of record, with the power to commit for contempt to themselves and all powers vested in a court of record before the constitution came into force (Article 126(2)).

3. The general rule that court proceedings shall be held in public, except where otherwise provided by the Constitution or ordered by a court in the interest of public morality, safety, or order (Article 126(3)).

4. The authority of the Superior Courts to issue orders and directions necessary to enforce any judgment, decree, or order within their jurisdiction (Article 126(4)).

These sections collectively define the structure, powers, and procedural principles governing the Superior Courts (Article 126, CHAPTER ELEVEN, p.108).
retrieved_contexts:
(1) The Judiciary shall consist of -
(a) the Superior Courts of Judicature comprising -
(i) the Supreme Court;
(ii) the Court of Appeal; and
(iii) the High Court and Regional Tribunals.
(b) such lower courts or tribunals as Parliament may by law
establish.
(2) The Superior Courts shall be superior courts of record and shall have
the power to commit for contempt to themselves and all such powers as
were vested in a court of record immediately before the coming into
force of this constitution.
(3) Except as otherwise provided in this Constitution or as may
otherwise be ordered by a court in the interest of public morality, public
safety or public order, the proceedings of every court shall be held in
public.
(4) In the exercise of the judicial power conferred on the Judiciary by
this Constitution or any other law, the Superior Courts may, in relation to
any matter within their jurisdiction, issue such orders and directions as
may be necessary to ensure the enforcement of any judgement, decree or
order of those courts.
reference: The main sections cover the Supreme Court (including its supervisory jurisdiction, power to review decisions, and powers of a Single Justice), the Court of Appeal (composition and qualifications of justices, and powers of a Single Justice), the High Court (composition, qualifications, jurisdiction, and supervisory jurisdiction), and Regional Tribunals (establishment, composition, qualifications, and jurisdiction). Additionally, sections address appointment, retirement, removal, and service conditions of justices and tribunal members.

user_input: What power does the First President under the Constitution have regarding laws within twelve months of assuming office?
response: The First President under the Constitution has the power, within twelve months after assuming office, to make provisions by constitutional instrument for repealing, modifying, adding to, or adapting any law to bring it into accord with the provisions of the Constitution or otherwise to give effect to the Constitution (Part III - The Judiciary, Section 30, p.207).
retrieved_contexts:
The First President under this Constitution may, at any time within
twelve months after assuming office as President, by constitutional
instrument, make such provision as may appear necessary for repealing,
modifying, adding to or adapting any law for bringing it into accord with
the provisions of this Constitution or otherwise for giving effect to this
Constitution.
reference: The First President may, at any time within twelve months after assuming office as President, by constitutional instrument, make provision for repealing, modifying, adding to or adapting any law for bringing it into accord with the provisions of the Constitution or otherwise for giving effect to the Constitution.

user_input: What is the voting requirement for matters in Parliament according to the Constitution?
response: The voting requirement for matters in Parliament according to the Constitution is that matters shall be determined by the votes of the majority of members present and voting, with at least half of all the members of Parliament present (Chapter TEN, Article 104, Section 1, p.97).
retrieved_contexts:
(1) Except as otherwise provided in this Constitution, matters in
Parliament shall be determined by the votes of the majority of members
present and voting, with at least half of all the members of Parliament
present.
(2) The Speaker shall have neither an original nor casting vote.
(3) Where the votes on any motion are equal it shall be taken to be lost.
(4) Where Parliament is considering a bill to amend the Constitution, or
where the voting is in relation to the election or removal of any person
under this Constitution or under any other law, voting shall be in secret.
(5) A member who is a party to or a partner in a firm which is a party to
a contract with the Government shall declare his interest and shall not
vote on any question relating to the contract.
reference: Matters in Parliament shall be determined by the votes of the majority of members present and voting, with at least half of all the members of Parliament present.
